title: Chapter House Books
author: Christen Arbogast
summary: Christen Arbogast, an assistant headmaster at Archway Trivium, reviews the Chapter House children's book sets curated by Joshua and Hannah Centers and uses them to argue that what families seeking alternative schools sense is missing is Western culture itself. Opening from John Senior's warning that modern societies have been living on depleted cultural capital, she presents the sets as a 'cultural lifeboat' drawing on the fountainheads of Athens, Rome, and Jerusalem. She praises the clothbound, illustrated volumes as deliberately anti-ephemeral, contrasting the experience of reading them with popular series like Dog Man and Captain Underpants. The first series gathers Aesop, Greek myths, and European history stories designed to form an age-appropriate moral imagination, while the second, Heroes and Wonders, moves from Genesis to Beowulf with few pictures so children imagine the myths rather than receiving them through Marvel-style visuals. Her closing move turns the books' difficult vocabulary into a virtue: because children cannot read them alone, they foster the shared experience of being read to by those who love them.

The Chapter House sets' physical beauty is part of the argument, positioning durable, illustrated books as an antidote to ephemeral popular children's series.
Read-aloud fables and myths are presented as forming a child's moral imagination and delivering wisdom more directly than information sources like ChatGPT.
The Heroes and Wonders series uses minimal illustration so children build imaginative engagement with myths instead of absorbing film and franchise versions.
Antiquated, polysyllabic vocabulary makes the stories hard for children to read alone, which the reviewer treats as an invitation to shared family reading.
quotes: Today, many families flock to alternative schools in large part, because they sense that something is missing in their child’s education. What is actually missing is Western Culture. More specifically, it is in the stories passed down that originate from the three great fountainheads of Western Civilization: Athens, Rome, and Jerusalem.

The Chapter House Series curates a beautifully bound cultural lifeboat for families, and I do mean beautiful. It is quite rewarding sitting down with my children to hold a clothbound hardback book, filled with beautiful illustrations and even more beautiful words. This is the type of experience that cannot be replicated with Dog Man or Captain Underpants. Aesthetically, the set is consciously anti-ephemeral and deserves a lasting place on the family bookshelf.

In Chapter 1, Joshua and Hannah Centers curate famous stories from Aesop’s Fables, Greek Myths, and European history. As they address in the companion essays, these works for younger children begin to form a moral imagination appropriate to a child’s age. This does not mean that the stories are dumbed down. The stories are meant to be read aloud, and it is in that magical process that a child’s imagination hitches onto the words to understand why it is dangerous to let a camel slowly into your tent.

It is in these stories that children receive more than just cultural knowledge; they receive Wisdom, precisely because the story encapsulates readily available truth faster than ChatGPT. In sitting down with my children to read these stories, I am amazed how the spoken word, which barely holds onto existence in small speech sounds, can lastingly temper a child’s heart toward Virtue.

In a culture saturated with depictions of mythology through the lens of Marvel, or indeed now with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, children interact with these stories visually first and narratively second. Even worse, their knowledge of myth is wrong or irreverent anachronistic (looking at you, Percy Jackson). The “Heroes and Wonder” selections offer a genuine reading with few pictures, for each child to develop an imaginative interaction with some of the oldest myths of our heritage.

Finally, many of these stories are too difficult for children to read on their own. The vocabulary at times is antiquated and polysyllabic in the best way. This provides, however, that other precious treasure of reading, the shared experience. What a wonderful gift for a child’s soul to be nurtured with beautiful stories read aloud by those they love.
